body:
We make Kiron, so weigh this accordingly. Everything here about Fitbod comes from its App Store listing, its help center, Garage Gym Reviews' hands-on review and recent App Store reviews, checked November 15, 2026. Everything about Kiron describes version 1.2.

People look for a Fitbod alternative for one of two reasons. The price went up and there's no free plan to drop down to. Or they have a plan, from a coach, a book or ChatGPT, and Fitbod keeps handing them its own.

Below: where Fitbod is still the better app, what Kiron (that's us) does differently, and how to leave without losing your logged workouts, whichever app you pick.

Fitbod or Kiron: the short answer

  • Stay with Fitbod if you like opening the app to a fresh workout, you log on an Apple Watch or Wear OS watch, or you still pay an older, lower price.
  • Switch to Kiron if the price is the problem (Kiron is {{kiron:price-annual}}; Fitbod's yearly plan is $95.99 for new subscribers), or you want to follow one plan, your own or one of 36 ready-made programs, with your runs in the same calendar.
  • Try Hevy's free plan or Boostcamp's free programs if you'd rather not pay at all.

Bottom line: Fitbod is built to choose your workouts. If you'd rather choose them yourself, or you already have a plan to follow, you're paying for the part you don't use.

What Fitbod costs now, and what reviewers complain about

Fitbod's own help center lists $15.99 a month or $95.99 a year, with a 7-day free trial for new users and no free plan after it. The US App Store still shows the older $12.99 and $79.99 prices too, so what you pay can depend on when you joined. A lifetime membership exists only as an occasional promotion.

Price is also the biggest theme in Fitbod's recent low-star reviews. Of its 500 most recent US App Store reviews (July 19 to November 13, 2026), 170 gave one to three stars, and 84 of those mention the price, billing or the lack of a free option. These are keyword counts, so treat them as approximate.

The second theme is control. More than 20 of the 170 are about the workouts Fitbod picks: the same exercises month after month, weights that don't fit, or the app overriding what the reviewer wanted. "It wants to have all the control," wrote one (1 star, November 2026). Fitbod's help center explains part of this: edits to a suggested workout are replaced if the suggestion refreshes before you tap Start Workout, and a workout syncing in from another app, or a change to your equipment or settings, can set off a refresh.

Two newer complaints: three low-star reviews from September and October say Fitbod's new Beta Coach suggested weights or reps that didn't fit (several five-star reviewers like it), and 11 of the 170 mention the Apple Watch, mostly in October and November, several saying an update broke it. If the Watch is your reason for leaving, Kiron won't help: it doesn't have a Watch app.

What Fitbod still does better

  • No planning at all. Open it and a session is ready, built from your history, your equipment and which muscles have recovered. With Kiron, you pick a plan first.
  • A long track record. Fitbod has about 290,000 ratings on the US App Store, averaging 4.8. Kiron is new and has a small user base.
  • Watch apps. Fitbod has an Apple Watch app and a Wear OS app. Kiron has neither; it reads your heart rate from Apple Health or Health Connect after a workout.
  • Recovery that counts your other training. Fitbod's muscle recovery already counts workouts that sync in from Apple Health, Health Connect, Fitbit or Strava. Kiron counts other apps' workouts too, through Apple Health or Health Connect, so this isn't a reason to switch.
  • A longer trial. Fitbod gives you 7 days free. Kiron has {{kiron:trial}}.
  • Video demos. Fitbod's exercises come with multi-angle video; most of Kiron's have an animated demo instead.

A new workout every session, or one plan you keep

Fitbod is a generator. You tell it your goal, your equipment and how often you train, and it decides what each session contains. You can build and save workouts of your own, and its listing says it learns from your edits, but choosing is the app's job, and its suggestions keep moving as your history changes.

Kiron runs one plan. Each day's workout comes from the plan, on a calendar, on the training days you pick, and it stays put until you change it. The Add a program screen has four ways in:

  • Choose a preset program. There are 36, filtered by goal, days, equipment and level, from a Beginner 5×5 and wave-loading strength with training maxes to hypertrophy splits, Beginner 5K, a marathon and a Sprint Triathlon.
  • Import a plan. Paste it as text, from ChatGPT, Claude, a coach or a website, or take or choose a photo of it. Kiron turns it into a scheduled program with sets, reps and rest, and keeps its phases if it has them. There's no PDF upload: paste the PDF's text or use a screenshot.
  • Build one with Kiron. Answer a few questions and it designs a program for you.
  • Start from scratch. Pick your days and add your own exercises.

Because the plan is fixed, a missed day doesn't quietly disappear. Today offers to move it to the next free day (Move to Thursday, say), or Pick a day or Skip, and when you've missed several, Push plan back, Pick days or Skip them. If your plan came from a chatbot, here's how to turn a ChatGPT workout plan into a program you can track, checks included.

Changing today without rewriting the plan

Both apps can change a single session. Fitbod's Training Session Mods change today's length and equipment, and its Swap menu changes the muscle focus. In Kiron, you tap Adjust today's workout:

  • Change the duration. Shorter drops extras, pairs accessories into supersets, then trims accessory sets; the main lifts stay. Longer adds sets where your week is behind.
  • Different equipment today, or one of your saved gyms, such as a hotel or a garage. Anything that needs equipment you don't have gets swapped.
  • Add to today: core, arms, shoulders, glutes, calves, a cardio finisher or stretching.

Everything on that sheet applies to today only and has an Undo, so tomorrow's workout is still the one your plan says. You can also swap a single exercise, just today or from now on. And when today's session leans on muscles that are still tired, Kiron says why and offers an easier version. For the background, see how long muscles need between workouts.

If you run, ride or swim as well

Fitbod is built around strength. Its help center describes cardio as something it adds to a strength session, and Garage Gym Reviews, which tested the app, says there are no cardio programs. A race plan has to live somewhere else.

In Kiron, runs, rides, swims and rows sit in the same plan and calendar as your lifting, with time and distance targets. Programs like Run + Lift, Half Marathon, Sprint Triathlon and Cycling Base schedule both, and a pasted plan keeps its runs. One limit: Kiron doesn't show pace in version 1.2. If running is your main event, our look at Runna's strength training covers the choice from the runner's side.

The App Store lists several prices for Fitbod: $12.99 and $15.99 a month, $79.99 and $95.99 a year, and older "Legacy Pricing" offers from $7.99 to $59.99. The table shows the $15.99 and $95.99 that Fitbod's help center lists; people who subscribed earlier may pay less. Prices vary by country and offer.

On the yearly plans, Kiron costs about half what Fitbod does. Kiron has no monthly plan, though. Its weekly plan is {{kiron:price-weekly}}, which comes to {{kiron:price-weekly-yearly}} if you keep it all year, more than twelve months of Fitbod's monthly plan. If you stay with Kiron, the yearly plan is the one to compare.

Leaving Fitbod without losing your history

One reviewer said the only thing that had kept them paying was not wanting to lose their history (1 star, October 2026). You don't have to lose it, whichever app you pick next.

Export first. In Fitbod, open Settings, then Export Workout Data, and save the file. It's a CSV of your logged sets, so it opens in any spreadsheet app; keep a copy even if you never import it anywhere. Our guide to exporting your workout history has the same steps for Strong, Hevy and other apps.

Kiron 1.2 can read that file. In Settings, tap Import from another app and choose it, and Kiron shows how it matched each exercise before it saves anything; you can remove an import later.

Other ways out, if Kiron isn't it either

  • Hevy has a free plan that logs unlimited workouts, with up to 4 routines. Hevy Pro, $23.99 a year or $74.99 once, adds Hevy Trainer, which builds a program from your goals, equipment and schedule and suggests when to add weight. If you liked Fitbod choosing for you and the price is the problem, look at Hevy Pro first. More in Hevy vs Kiron.
  • Boostcamp is free for 99 of its 132 coach-designed programs, the workout tracker, and as many programs of your own as you care to build. Pro is $59.99 a year.

FitnessAI, Gravl and Planfit work on Fitbod's idea, an AI that picks your sessions, so they're closer to Fitbod than Kiron is. FitnessAI sets each workout's exercises, sets, reps and weights, keeps sessions between 5 and 30 minutes, and has an Apple Watch app; Gravl and Planfit call themselves an AI personal trainer and an AI gym workout planner on the App Store. Each lists several prices there, with yearly plans from $59.99 to $89.99 for FitnessAI and Gravl and from $79.99 to $89.99 for Planfit, so check the paywall before a trial ends.

For more options, sorted by the job each app does, see our guide to workout apps for following a program.

Who should stay with Fitbod

  • You don't have a plan and don't want one. Being handed a balanced session is the point, and Fitbod has done it for years.
  • You log on your wrist. Fitbod has Apple Watch and Wear OS apps; Kiron has no Watch app.
  • You're on an older price. At $79.99 a year the gap to Kiron's yearly plan is smaller, and your history and settings are already in Fitbod.
  • Its picks suit you. If the complaints above don't match your experience, there's little reason to move.

Switch if you find yourself rebuilding its suggestions, following someone else's plan on the side, or keeping your runs in a second app.

Fitbod questions, answered

Is Fitbod free?

No. There's no free plan: the App Store listing offers 7 days free, then a monthly or yearly subscription. Some older guides describe three free workouts, but that isn't what the listing offers now.

How much is Fitbod now, and did the price go up?

New subscribers pay $15.99 a month or $95.99 a year, according to Fitbod's help center. Older reviews list $12.99 and $79.99, and the App Store still shows both pairs, so the price did rise. We couldn't find the date of the change on Fitbod's own pages.

Is there a Fitbod lifetime subscription?

Only now and then. Fitbod's help center says a lifetime membership is a promotion, available for short periods, and points people to its marketing emails to hear when it returns. The rest of the time, it's monthly or yearly.

Can I export my Fitbod workouts?

Yes: Settings, then Export Workout Data, which saves a CSV file. Our export guide covers what to do with it.

Is Fitbod worth it for beginners?

It can be, if you want the app to make every decision while you learn the movements; the videos help, and 7 free days is enough to judge its picks. Garage Gym Reviews, which tested it, scores it 3.9 out of 5. If you'd rather learn on a fixed program, a beginner barbell plan such as Kiron's Beginner 5×5 or Novice Linear Progression is the traditional start.

Is there an app like Fitbod but cheaper or free?

Free: Hevy's free plan, or Boostcamp's free coach programs. Still planned for you: Hevy Pro at $23.99 a year, which includes Hevy Trainer, or FitnessAI and Gravl, from $59.99 a year. Your own plan, runs included: Kiron at {{kiron:price-annual}}.

If Fitbod's price, or wanting to follow a plan instead of a fresh pick each day, is why you're here, try Kiron. Pick one of the 36 programs or paste the plan you already follow, and see your weeks laid out on the calendar. {{kiron:cta-sentence}} Get Kiron.

If you just want a free log, Hevy's free plan is the better call. And if you like what Fitbod does and can live with the price, staying is a perfectly good answer.
